title: The Gulf Stream carries 50 times the water of all the rivers flowing into the Atlantic
body: The Gulf Stream is a river inside the ocean: a current typically about **100 km wide** and 800 to 1,200 m deep that runs from the Gulf of Mexico through the Straits of Florida and up the coast of North America. Through the Florida Straits it moves about 30 million cubic metres of water a second, while all the rivers that empty into the Atlantic together manage about 0.6 million. Further on, as it passes south of Newfoundland, its flow reaches about 150 million cubic metres a second.

cover.alt: Visualisation of a globe centred on North America, with bright swirling streaks of ocean current curving north along the US east coast and off into the Atlantic

slides.alt: Animated globe of the western North Atlantic with ocean currents drawn as flowing white streaks: a bright ribbon runs out of the Gulf of Mexico, hugs the US east coast, then meanders east into the Atlantic, shedding swirling eddies.
slides.caption: Ocean surface currents computed from a model of 2005: the Gulf Stream is the bright ribbon pouring past Florida and up the coast before snaking out into the Atlantic.

slides.label: the current’s typical top speed, near the surface
slides.text: About 9 km/h. The flow is fastest at the surface and slows with depth.

slides.question: In the clip, swirls break away from the current. What are they?
slides.explanation: When one of the Gulf Stream’s meanders loops round and closes off, it breaks away as a separate spinning ring of water.
